This yields a maximum reproductive rate of 1 pup per year [Ri = 1 pup per year], documented across multiple populations occupying similar thermal regimes, reflecting the energetic constraints associated with sustaining the high body temperatures characteristic of active flight. The timing of these reproductive events is tightly linked to local temperature conditions; for instance, the gestation period has been measured at 45 days [tg = 45 days] under the stable thermal conditions of roosting chambers that maintain an average temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This relatively short gestation, combined with the single-pup litter, suggests a strategy that prioritizes investment in each offspring over high fecundity.

The duration of maternal dependence also appears to be brief relative to other bats of similar size; weaning occurs at 45 days after birth [tx = 45 days after birth] under the same thermal conditions that characterize maternal roosts at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. At this point, the juvenile is capable of independent foraging, though it may continue to roost with the mother for some additional weeks.

The maximum wet weight attained by adult females is 5.89 grams [Wwi = 5.89 grams], representing more than a doubling of the birth mass and placing Hipposideros pomona among the smaller members of its genus. This adult mass is typically reached well before the onset of reproductive activity. Regarding lifespan, the longest-lived individuals recorded in wild populations have survived for 13 years [am = 13 years], a remarkable longevity given their diminutive size at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This extended lifespan is likely linked to the slow pace of life characteristic of many tropical bat species and is achieved under the same warm roost temperatures of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] that facilitate the species' other physiological processes.

The progression from birth to sexual maturation spans a considerable period in the life of a female Pomona roundleaf bat. Puberty is attained at 730 days since birth [tp = 730 days since birth], meaning that females typically do not become reproductively mature until they are roughly two years old at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This delayed onset of sexual maturation, measured in populations inhabiting stable thermal environments maintained at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], aligns with patterns observed in other bats that exhibit slow life histories and extended parental care. The post-weaning period is therefore prolonged, as juveniles must accumulate sufficient body reserves and foraging experience before they can successfully gestate and rear a pup of their own. This developmental bottleneck likely contributes to the low annual reproductive output of the species.

Lactation imposes substantial energetic demands on female bats, and the suckling juvenile depends entirely on the mother's milk until nutritional independence is achieved. Field studies have confirmed that the time since birth at weaning is 45 days [tx = 45 days] for pups born in maternity colonies where the ambient temperature is consistently maintained at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. During this pre-weaning period, juvenile growth is rapid, with the pup transitioning from a mass of approximately 2.3 grams at birth to a fully weaned sub-adult that is nearly capable of self-sufficiency. The ecological context of these life-history traits is instructive: as a species dependent on warm, humid caves and abandoned mines for roosting, the Pomona roundleaf bat's reproductive schedule is finely tuned to the thermal stability its roosts provide, ensuring that both gestation and lactation occur under optimal thermal conditions. The combined influence of its modest body size, extended lifespan, and delayed maturation underscores the slow life-history strategy of this species, which is consistent with predictions based on metabolic scaling theory for tropical insectivorous mammals.
